query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, controlled amount of titanium into the W–Cu composite to enable the in situ formation of fine TiC particles at the W and W–Cu interfaces will suppress phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity under high heat‐flux and irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite comprising discrete tungsten particles or an interconnected tungsten ligament network embedded in a copper matrix that exhibits phase separation and interfacial void formation during high-temperature heat transfer and irradiation.
generation.intervention: Add a controlled minor titanium content during powder mixing so that during spark plasma sintering the Ti reacts (with residual carbon or added carbon) to form finely dispersed TiC at the tungsten phase and along the tungsten–copper interfaces.
generation.conditions: Process using spark plasma sintering to consolidate the Ti-doped composite; then subject the material to service conditions representative of plasma-facing joints, namely high heat flux (e.g., ~10 MW/m² or similar), elevated temperatures (up to ~1000 °C), and exposure to irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formed, nano- to sub-micron TiC particles that decorate or pin the grain boundaries and interfaces between W and Cu.
generation.mechanism: The formation of TiC particles at the interface reduces interfacial energy and acts as a barrier to grain boundary migration and void coalescence. This pinning effect stabilizes the microstructure by suppressing phase separation and interfacial void formation, thus preserving a continuous pathway for phonon and electron transport, which enhances overall thermal conductivity under extreme service conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated composite, the Ti-modified composite will exhibit a more uniform microstructure with fewer voids and reduced phase separation. This improved interfacial stability is predicted to lead to a measurable increase in thermal conductivity during operation under high heat flux and irradiation.
generation.baseline: The untreated W–Cu composite in which significant phase separation and interfacial voids lower the thermal conductivity, especially under thermal cycling and irradiation stresses.
generation.boundary: Applicable to W–Cu composites processed via powder metallurgy (e.g., spark plasma sintering) and intended for plasma-facing applications where operating temperatures, heat fluxes, and irradiation conditions are similar to those in fusion reactor joints between tungsten plasma-facing elements and copper-based cooling components.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal titanium content required to form an effective and continuous TiC dispersion without adversely affecting other mechanical or thermal properties remains to be determined. There is also some uncertainty regarding the magnitude of the thermal conductivity improvement and any secondary effects such as changes in residual stresses or ductility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set with the controlled titanium addition expected to yield in situ TiC formation and one control set without titanium. Process both sets under identical spark plasma sintering conditions. Subject the samples to simulated service conditions including high heat flux, elevated temperature cycling, and ion irradiation. Characterize the microstructure using SEM/EDS and HRTEM to assess phase separation and void density. Measure thermal conductivity (using techniques such as laser flash analysis or non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations) before and after exposure.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (void density, interface coherence, TiC dispersion) via SEM/EDS/HRTEM
Thermal conductivity measurements under relevant heat flux
Comparative performance under simulated irradiation doses
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in phase separation and interfacial void formation as compared to the control, or if their thermal conductivity under high-temperature and irradiation conditions is not measurably improved relative to the untreated composite, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The W-based composite having uniformly distributed TiC within the grains and along the grain boundaries can withstand heat flux as high as 200 MW/m2, which is nearly 100% higher than the flux sustained by pure W. An increase in the amount of the evenly distributed TiC in the W matrix (inside the grains and along the boundaries) also increases the hardness creep strength and modulus of elasticity, , . The presence of TiC in the grains and on the grain boundaries also favors fusion applications, as it increases the recrystallization temperature and irradiation resistance. TiC does not have a significant effect on the deuterium retention behavior of W-based materials, . The dispersion of carbides in the grain boundaries of W leads to grain boundary strengthening and provides some resistance to grain boundary migration at elevated temperatures. Therefore, TiC is considered to be beneficial in high-temperature and plasma-facing alloys. The volume fraction of TiC in the xWs samples determined by analyzing the SEM images was found to vary from 1.1 to 8.5% (Table S3).
